title: Gods on the Tablets
short: po-se-da-o (Poseidon), di-we and di-wo (Zeus), e-ra (Hera), di-wo-nu-so (Dionysus), e-ma-a2 (Hermes) and a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja (Mistress Athena) appear by name.
trouble: Students assume the Olympians were invented later. Several are named on the tablets, though we know little of the myths told about them then.

blocks.html: Among the words you can now read (Endings You Can See) are names that every reader of Greek myths knows. The tablets record offerings to gods, and many of those gods are the Olympians of later Greece, named centuries before Homer.
The tablets name po-se-da-o (Poseidon), di-we and di-wo (Zeus, "to Zeus", "of Zeus"), e-ra (Hera), di-wo-nu-so (Dionysus), e-ma-a2 (Hermes) and a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja (Mistress Athena), among others.

blocks.name: sc-tablet
blocks.cap: An extract from Pylos tablet Tn 316: gold vessels to Zeus, Hera and Drimios, son of Zeus.

items: Poseidon receives many offerings at Pylos; he seems more important there than Zeus.
Dionysus was once thought to be a late arrival in Greece. His name is on tablets from Pylos and Chania.
Drimios, called the son of Zeus on Tn 316, is unknown from later Greek religion.
Potnia, "Lady" or "Mistress", appears often, sometimes with a place or a name, as in a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja, which most read as Mistress Athena.

blocks.html: The gods turn up at several palaces: Zeus, Hera and Poseidon at Pylos; Mistress Athena and others at Knossos; Dionysus at Chania and Pylos. Some offering lists are dated by month, so the tablets also tell us a little about the religious year, though not what the gods were believed to do.

Why are we confident these are gods, not people with the same names? The context: these names receive offerings of oil, honey, gold vessels or animals, often at named shrines, in lists alongside words like te-o (god) and po-ti-ni-ja (lady). And the names match later Greek gods through the regular spelling rules.

Assuming the Olympians were invented later, in Homer's time or after. Several are named on the tablets, though we know little of the myths told about them then; the tablets give names and offerings, not stories. Check: separate what the tablets show (a name and an offering) from what later myths add (family stories, adventures).

blocks.title: To or of?
blocks.q: An offering list begins with di-we. Is the offering to Zeus or of Zeus?
steps: The dative marks the receiver: "to Zeus".

blocks.title: Read a name
blocks.q: Read 𐀁𐀨 and name the goddess.
steps: e is the vowel sign; ra is r + a.
h is not written, so e-ra is Hera.

blocks.html: The reading of e-ma-a2 as Hermes (e-ma-ha) is widely accepted, but the a2 sign makes the exact form a little uncertain. A few other names, like Drimios, have no later Greek match at all.
